options.content: ### ② SATURATION

**PSI (/proc/pressure/cpu)**

- Rising: tasks are queuing for CPU. This is real saturation, even if utilization looks moderate.
- Near zero: no CPU contention, even if utilization is high.

panels.title: S · PSI (/proc/pressure/cpu)
panels.description: Time tasks spent stalled waiting for CPU

options.content:
### ③ UTILIZATION

*Use the Core view and CPU core buttons at the top: per core, or all cores together.*

**%usr (application code)**

- High on all cores: the app is CPU-bound (game logic, move validation, JSON handling). Expect move latency (SLI-3) to rise at the same time.
- Low: the app is not computing heavily, so the CPU is not the bottleneck.

**%sys (kernel work)**

- High: the kernel is busy handling many syscalls, network packets or context switches, typically many WebSocket connections sending small messages.
- Low: kernel overhead is not a problem.

panels.title: U · %usr per core
panels.description: CPU time running application code

panels.title: U · %sys per core
panels.description: CPU time in the kernel (syscalls, networking, disk)

options.content:
**%iowait (waiting on disk)**

- High: tasks are waiting for storage, so the problem is the disk and not the CPU.
- Low: storage is not making the CPU wait.

**%steal (hypervisor, VMs only)**

- High: the host is taking CPU time from the VM (noisy neighbour). Nothing inside the VM can fix it, and test results become unreliable.
- Low: the VM gets the CPU it expects.

panels.title: U · %iowait per core
panels.description: CPU idle while waiting on disk

panels.title: U · %steal per core
panels.description: CPU time taken by the hypervisor (VMs only)

options.content:
**Top 10 CPU usage**

- One process dominates: that process is the main CPU consumer and the first suspect.
- Load spread evenly: no single culprit, so look at overall capacity.

**CPU low but latency high: the bottleneck is not the CPU. Move to memory, disk, network, or the database and locks.**

panels.title: U · Top 10 CPU usage (processes)
panels.description: The processes consuming the most CPU

options.content: ### ① ERRORS

**dmesg | grep -i killed**

- Any entry: the OOM killer terminated a process. This is a hard failure, and a sudden drop in SLI-1 or SLI-5 at the same time confirms it.
- Empty: no process was killed for memory.

panels.title: E · OOM kills (dmesg | grep -i killed)
panels.description: The kernel killed a process because RAM ran out (OOM killer)

options.content: ### ② SATURATION

**so (pages written to disk)**

- Sustained above 0: the kernel is under memory pressure and latency will rise with it.
- 0: no memory pressure.

**si (pages read from disk)**

- Sustained above 0: processes are already being delayed because their memory sits on disk.
- 0: processes are not waiting on swapped memory.

**majflt/s**

- High: active data is not in RAM, so every access is slow, which indicates a memory shortage.
- Low: the working set fits in RAM.

panels.title: S · si / so
panels.description: Pages moved from / to disk per second

panels.title: S · majflt/s
panels.description: Pages that had to be read from disk

options.content: ### ③ UTILIZATION

**available**

- Shrinking steadily during a long test: likely a memory leak (for example game rooms or WebSocket objects never released).
- Low free but high available: normal. Linux uses spare RAM as cache, so free always looks low and should not trigger an alert.
- High and stable: memory is not the bottleneck.

**Swap used**

- Rising: the system ran out of RAM and is pushing memory to disk.
- Zero: no memory pressure so far.

**Swap at 0 and available high: memory is not the bottleneck.**

panels.title: U · available (free -m)
panels.description: RAM that apps can still use without swapping

panels.title: U · Swap used (free -m)
panels.description: Disk being used as extra memory

options.content:
**Top 10 RAM usage**

- One process keeps growing: that process is the likely leak.
- Memory returns after players leave: the usage is normal load, not a leak.

panels.title: U · Top 10 RAM usage (processes)
panels.description: The processes consuming the most memory

options.content: ### ① ERRORS

**rx / tx errors (added)**

- Above 0: packets are failing on the interface.
- 0: no errors on the network interface.

panels.title: E · rx / tx errors per second
panels.description: Packets that failed on the interface

options.content: ### ② SATURATION

**rxdrop/s, txdrop/s**

- Above 0: buffers are full and the host cannot process packets fast enough. High %sys at the same time supports this.
- 0: the interface and kernel are keeping up.

**TcpRetransSegs**

- Rising: packet loss or congestion between client and server. Players on bad networks will show high latency (SLI-3) and disconnects (SLI-5).
- Rising only as the number of players rises: a network limit or connection pressure under load.
- Flat: the network path is healthy.

panels.title: S · rxdrop/s, txdrop/s
panels.description: Packets discarded because buffers were full

panels.title: S · TcpRetransSegs (nstat)
panels.description: TCP segments resent after loss

options.content: ### ③ UTILIZATION

**rx / tx throughput (added)**

- Close to the bandwidth limit (red dashed line): the NIC or instance bandwidth cap is reached.
- Far below the limit: bandwidth is not the constraint.

panels.title: U · rx / tx throughput vs Max NIC bandwidth
panels.description: Data received and sent per second

options.content: ### ② SATURATION

**await (added)**

- High: requests are waiting on the disk, so latency rises.
- Low: the disk answers quickly, even if %util looks high.

**Queue depth (aqu-sz) (added)**

- Above 1 on a single disk: requests are queueing.
- Near 0: no queue.

panels.title: S · await
panels.description: Average time a request waits and is served

panels.title: S · Queue depth (aqu-sz)
panels.description: Requests waiting on the disk

options.content: ### ③ UTILIZATION

**%util**

- Near 100% on an HDD: the disk is saturated.
- Near 100% on SSD/NVMe: not necessarily a problem, because these disks handle requests in parallel. Judge by request latency (await) instead.
- Low: the disk is not busy.

panels.title: U · %util
panels.description: % of time the disk had at least one request in progress

options.content:
**r/s, w/s**

- Close to the volume's IOPS limit (red dashed line): the IOPS cap is reached, typical on cloud volumes.
- Far below the limit: IOPS are not the constraint.

**rkB/s, wkB/s**

- Close to the bandwidth limit (red dashed line) while IOPS is low: large transfers hit the throughput cap.
- Far below the limit: throughput is not the constraint.

panels.title: U · r/s, w/s vs Max IOPS
panels.description: Reads and writes completed per second

panels.title: U · rkB/s, wkB/s vs Max disk bandwidth
panels.description: Data read and written per second (throughput)

options.content:
**Combined reading**

- %iowait high and %util high: storage is the bottleneck.
- %iowait high but %util low: the wait is probably on network storage or another device.
### ① ERRORS

**Filesystem device errors (added)**

- Any value: the filesystem reports a device error, so writes may fail.
- 0: no device errors.

panels.title: E · Filesystem device errors
panels.description: The filesystem reports a device error

options.content: ### ② SATURATION

**Hours until full (added)**

- Under ~24 h: the partition will fill soon at the current rate.
- Rising or stable: no growth problem.

panels.title: S · Hours until full (6 h trend)
panels.description: Estimated time before the partition is full at the current rate

options.content: ### ③ UTILIZATION

**Use% (df -h)**

- Above ~90%: the disk will fill soon. Writes will fail and the app or database can crash.
- Growing fast during the test: excessive logging or data generation under load.

**Inodes (df -i)**

- Near 100% while Use% is low: too many small files (logs, temp files, sessions).

panels.title: U · Use% (df -h) per partition
panels.description: % of space used

panels.title: U · Inodes (df -i) used per partition
panels.description: File slots left (shown as % used)
